The VAWT design allows adjusting the blade angle from 60° to 180° to adapt the turbine's characteristics to different wind speeds.
The maximum power output of 40.5 W was achieved at a rotational speed of 100 rpm and a blade angle of 180°.
The maximum torque of 4.8 Nm was achieved at the lowest simulated rotational speed of 20 rpm and a blade angle of 100°.
The maximum power coefficient of 0.082 was achieved at a tip-speed ratio (TSR) of 2.1 and a blade angle of 100°.
The 180°, 140°, and 100° blade angle settings had relatively similar maximum power outputs, around 35-40 W, while the 60° setting had a noticeably lower maximum power of 19.5 W.
The torque coefficient showed a non-linear decrease as the rotational speed increased, with the maximum value occurring at a blade angle of 100° despite the maximum torque being at 180°.
The turbine's height can range from 206 mm (for 30° blade angle) to 700 mm (for 180° blade angle), while the rotor diameter is almost constant at 700 mm.
The computational mesh used in the CFD simulations contained 2.8 million elements with an average element quality of 0.76196.
The simulations were performed using the ANSYS Fluent software with the k-omega SST turbulence model.
The CFD simulations were run for two full rotations of the turbine, with a time step corresponding to a 2-degree rotation.
The study compared the CFD results to expected VAWT performance characteristics, finding trends consistent with typical VAWT behavior.
The simplified turbine geometry and single wind speed of 10 m/s used in the CFD simulations may not capture the full operating range of the VAWT.
The variable swept area design of the VAWT allows it to adapt its characteristics to different wind speeds and protect the rotor from damage in high wind conditions.

Vertical axis wind turbines (VAWTs) are more flexible to wind direction, have a smaller footprint, generate less noise, and can operate at lower wind speeds compared to horizontal axis wind turbines (HAWTs).
The overall efficiency of a wind turbine is affected by both aerodynamic efficiency and mechanical/electrical losses, with the aerodynamic efficiency being one of the key factors.
